questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) List two Terms according to Quality.

(ii) Define Language. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** According to quality, terms are **positive** (they state the presence of a quality, e.g. "honest") and **negative** (they state the absence of it, e.g. "dishonest", "non-smoker"). (Some textbooks add a third kind, privative terms, e.g. "blind".)

**(ii)** **Language** is a system of conventional signs (spoken or written words, gestures, symbols) used by a community to express and communicate thoughts, ideas and feelings. It is the vehicle of thought.
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) What determines the Distribution of Terms in a Proposition?

(ii) What is a Modal Proposition? (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The distribution of terms is determined by the **quantity** and the **quality** of the proposition. Quantity governs the subject: a universal proposition distributes its subject. Quality governs the predicate: a negative proposition distributes its predicate. So A distributes the subject only, E both terms, I neither, O the predicate only.

**(ii)** A **modal proposition** states the manner (mode) in which the predicate belongs to the subject: necessity, possibility, impossibility or contingency. Examples: "It is possible that it will rain"; "All men must die".
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
O Level Logic - propositions and their types

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Explain the following concepts as used in Symbolic Logic:

(i) Variables.

(ii) Braces. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Variables** are letters (p, q, r, s ...) that stand for any proposition (or term), whatever it may say; each can take the value true or false. They allow us to study the form of an argument and not its content.

**(ii) Braces** { } are grouping symbols used, with parentheses ( ) and brackets [ ], to show which parts of a compound formula belong together, so as to avoid ambiguity. In the usual order, parentheses are innermost, then brackets, then braces.
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) State the relationship between the "A" and "E" Propositions on the Square of Opposition.

(ii) Define an Argument. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A and E propositions with the same subject and predicate are **contraries**: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false. If one is true, the other is false; if one is false, the other is undetermined (doubtful).

**(ii)** An **argument** is a group of propositions in which one, the conclusion, is claimed to follow from, or to be supported by, the others, the premises. It is the expression in language of the act of reasoning.
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) Briefly explain what a Modus Ponens Argument is.

(ii) Name any two Fallacies of Relevance. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** **Modus Ponens** is a valid mixed hypothetical syllogism whose conditional major premise is followed by a minor premise that **affirms the antecedent**, and whose conclusion affirms the consequent: If p then q; p; therefore q. Example: "If it rains, the road is wet. It rains. Therefore the road is wet."

**(ii)** Any two: **appeal to force** (ad baculum), **appeal to pity** (ad misericordiam), **appeal to the people** (ad populum), **argument against the person** (ad hominem), **irrelevant conclusion** (ignoratio elenchi).
